utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, I understand there is a matter that you wish to raise in the absence of the next witness. What is it?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is this, Mr. Robinson: A physician's report. I hope that you have it before you, that you received it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I should just -- let me just stop you there. We haven't received any physician's report. Do you reason the report from Dr. Falke?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No. What I meant was the report by three prominent specialists who examined me on the 4th of November. That means ten days ago. And I would like to mention that in their report they present a joint view, a joint position by the consortium of physicians, and they say, among other things: "The patient's state of health has not stabilised and that complications are possible. [In English] Accordingly, the patient should be prescribed -- prescribed a period of rest; i.e., the suspension of all physical and mental activities for a minimum period of six weeks, which will probably reduce or at least stabilise the symptoms."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, the Chamber is not privy to that report. If you want us to make a determination on anything that arises from that report, then you should submit it to us and we'll consider it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It is being copied at the moment by Professor Rakic, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Well, we wouldn't be able to consider that at this particular time. We haven't seen that report at all, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why my microphone is being switched off all the time. But that is the problem, where the problem lies. You haven't seen the report, and in the report by Dr. Falke it says that I was not here on Friday, as it says, due to exhaustion. Dr. Falke knows full well that for several months now I have serious health problems. I don't need to complain about them, nor is it my intention to complain about anything here before you. I was in Bronovo Hospital a few times for examinations, and he knows full well the kind of problems that I'm suffering from. The doctors who came to see me came two months after not having provided me with adequate and proper treatment to make note of what they noted. And I should like to stress that we're talking about highly acclaimed experts, professionals from Russia, France, and Serbia. So this kind of contradiction to Dr. Falke's report is not acceptable in any way, and I do feel that the position taken by the doctors must be respected, especially as they are serious problems that are involved. And otherwise I would like to remind you that even if I were in full health, which I am not, unfortunately, in the decision by the Appeals Chamber, the ruling made with respect to the joining of three indictments or a joinder of three indictments, in point 27 it says quite clearly the following: "[In English] As has been shown to be necessary in all long trials before this Tribunal, the Trial Chamber will from time to time have to take a break in the hearing of evidence to enable the parties to marshal their forces and, if need be, for the unrepresented accused to rest from the work involved." [Interpretation] In all these years -- well, I don't want to count them, but I have never been accorded anything like that let alone the fact that this was binding on the Trial Chamber and that the other side -- "... not to become unmanageable by overloading the Trial Chamber and the Defence with unnecessary material."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, as I indicated, the Chamber is not privy to that report. We have not seen it. If you wish us to see it, then you must ensure that we -- that we get it. And if you have any submission to make arising out of that report, then -- then you may make it. But it is pointless continuing the discussion on the basis of a report which is not before the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I have brought up this subject matter and quoted the position taken by the physicians, but it's up to you what you do next. I'm not going to raise the question any more. The fact that you have not been apprised of it, you should have been informed because the Registrar is duty-bound to inform you about matters like that. It is the Registrar who is in charge of health matters and other similar problems.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you must ensure that we get the report. You are the party involved. Let us have the report and we'll see --

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: I do have copies here that have been prepared. I've got the full bundles here with the original language. I don't know whether you've got those there before the -- maybe these are the better reports for the Court to have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Kay has been good enough to provide what appears to be the report to which you have referred. We are seeing it now for the first time. We will look at it, but you must make it clear to the Chamber what it is that you wish the Chamber to do arising from this report.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nothing other than asking the Trial Chamber not to ignore what it says in the doctors' report, and that means that they said quite specifically suspension of all physical and mental activities [In English] for a minimum period of six weeks.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well, Mr. Milosevic. The Chamber has the report now. We will look at the report and give consideration to the submission that you have made.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I would like to make it clear at this stage that I don't understand any motion to have been made other than for the Trial Chamber to look at the documents. In my opinion, if these are said to give rise to a need for this trial to be adjourned, then that would have to be the subject of a written motion. I don't think it's an appropriate matter to be considered on the basis of the oral submission that's been made so far in this case. I understand that's not the view of my colleagues, but I thought it right to make my position clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry, in which case that should be redacted. Well, can I, in those circumstances, invite the Court's attention to paragraph 6 of that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, we have that report. We have that report.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And possibly before the Court makes a decision, if it's minded to make this decision, to embark on a reading and consideration of the latest report provided, to deal with that paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No doubt that will be one of the matters that the Chamber will consider along with the consideration of the submissions from the accused. Call your next witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson. Mr. Robinson, in connection with this, I'm very grateful to Mr. Nice for moving that question. What it says there is not correct. There's probably some misunderstanding.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We are not going to discuss that now. Call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, just one sentence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I do not wish to have it discussed now. Are you deaf? Call your next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I probably am deaf.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, if you are, we'll see about that. Call the next witness.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But the fact that I'm deaf won't stop me from working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: No doubt that's to your credit.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The next witness is Husein Sarvanovic, Captain Husein Sarvanovic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, commence the examination.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Captain.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, would you please introduce yourself.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Husein Sarvanovic, captain of the army of Serbia and Montenegro, retired, born on the 14th of February, 1961, Modric municipality, Bosnia-Herzegovina. I am a citizen of Serbia and Montenegro. I completed my secondary military school in Sarajevo. After that, I served in Pirot as a junior officer. In 1992 I completed the higher military school and as an officer started working in Pirot. I continued my service in Surdulica, Prizren, and Leskovac, where I was retired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did you serve in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I served in Kosovo and Metohija from the 11th of May, 1998, until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What are you by ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'm a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what were you during the war in Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: During the war in Kosovo and Metohija, I was the commander of a motorised company in the 1st Battalion of the Prizren Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the map next to you --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And, gentlemen, that map was introduced into evidence during the testimony of -- or, rather, map already admitted during the testimony of General Djosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you show us on that map where you were and where your movements were in Kosovo and Metohija during that time.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: My unit was given its assignment for the region of Zur. The area of responsibility was Zur village and to the east, bordering on the village of Zur; to right or, rather, to the west, the Ceja [phoen] feature and mortar, 82-millimetre mortar unit in the village of Vrbnica at the border crossing with the Republic of Albania. And another rifle unit. And that is where I carried out my assignment with my original unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. You mentioned that among your unit you had a mortar platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I don't want to quote from the actual papers but in many places it says that our army shelled villages and towns. So I'm going to ask you to tell me, with that mortar platoon of yours, did you ever fire any shells?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could you explain to us how that came about, what the situation was, and what the target was.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Since the mortar platoon was within the composition of my company and I was in command of the platoon because there were no other available officers, high-ranking officers, the way in which the 82-millimetre mortars acted was this: As my position was at the command post, reconnoitering command post, I would go into action pursuant to orders from the commander. So we would prepare for targeting and then a fire point would be targeted from where shooting was coming from. We never targeted any other features or targets which were not military targets or, rather, targets used to fire at us from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So, Captain, what -- from what you've just said, it -- the following would emerge: Your position was a position next to the commander.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, next to the commander at the observation post.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the observation post. I see. Now, were you personally able to establish from which firing points your unit was being fired at?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, because next to me we had two scouts for reconnoitering purposes and reconnaissance and to tell us where the firing was coming from.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that you would target a feature or facility from which you were not fired at or our units were not fired at?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, we never did that nor did our unit ever receive orders to target facilities which were not used as fire points and points of fire towards our units.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did it ever happen that you would -- your shell would go amiss and you would hit a civilian feature by mistake? Did you ever miss your mark, in fact?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, that never happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. Captain, a document was introduced into evidence here which was mentioned in General Delic's testimony and then Colonel Vukovic's. It is a document that was entitled "Order for the reinforcement and support of MUP forces to break up the Siptar terrorist forces in the area of Orahovac, Suva Reka, and Velika Krusa." Are you acquainted with that document? And it's to be found in tab 2 of your binder. Otherwise, it was introduced and admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document meant nothing to me because I actually saw the document for the first time when I was in a proofing session with the lawyer here, and this is a classical order by a corps commander to brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But -- I know that, but were you able to find anywhere in that record, once you had studied it, the position of your particular unit mentioned or the activities that you had?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I was not able to find that anywhere in that order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, since we've established that point, explain this to us: During the events to which the order relates, did you take part in any combat action?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did take part in combat action, but pursuant to an order that I received from my combat group commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. Fine. Now, tell me this: Did you ever receive anybody else's order except an order from the command of your combat group?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Every time you went into action did you go into action exclusively pursuant to the order issued by the commander of your combat group?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your company and when we're dealing with the artillery weapons, mortars, and so on, was there any action where people would go into action of their own free will without having received orders?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, no action arbitrary of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the exhibit number of this document, Mr. Milosevic? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This document was admitted. It was D30, tab 356. It was used on the 30th of June, admitted on the 1st of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's D300 rather than 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you. D300.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, in connection with those activities, what your particular unit was doing.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: My unit, receiving its assignment from the commander of the combat group, supported and reinforced MUP forces - that's the assignment it was given in the army of Yugoslavia - in the breaking up and destruction of the Siptar terrorist forces along the axis of Orahovac-Suva Reka.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Bela Crkva is in the Orahovac municipality. Do you know Bela Crkva? Do you know the place?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, please, could this map of Bela Crkva be placed on the overhead projector. It is a large-scale map, so everything is clearly indicated. Captain, can you say what this map represents? Can you explain it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is a map of the village of Bela Crkva. On it we can see the initial deployment. On it we can see the initial deployment of the forces of Combat Group 2 that was about to carry out its tasks, the direction from which the units came in order to carry out this task. Also, there is the line from which the group set off. It's about 700 to 1.000 metres away from the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, the indictment, in paragraph 66(b), alleges that on the 25th of March, 1999, or around that date, the forces of the FRY and Serbia surrounded and attacked the village of Bela Crkva, municipality of Orahovac. Were you there then at the time?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, that is not correct. On the 24th of March, between 1930 hours and 2000 hours, I went along the outskirts of the village of Bela Crkva and deployed the units in Brnjaca, which is about 700 to 1.000 metres away from the village of Bela Crkva. As I passed through, I did not have any problems in the village. It was peaceful. I spent the night in Brnjaca and I was disturbed. We could not get any proper rest because NATO aircraft were flying from the Republic of Albania towards the territory of Yugoslavia. The village of Brnjaca is a locality I left in the morning around 5.00, and I proceeded towards Orahovac and Velika Hoca from where I carried out the assignment given to me by the commander of the combat group. I note once again that there were no problems during my stay in Bela Crkva or during the course of the night.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any activity of any other unit in Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It is stated here that many villagers from Bela Crkva fled along the Belaja river and that they were forced to seek shelter and that the forces of Serbia opened fire, killing 12 persons. Do you know anything about this?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This assertion is not correct. There was no activity. I claim that my own unit never did any such thing, and I have not heard of any unit having done anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on it is stated that the forces of the FRY and Serbia then ordered the men and older boys to strip and then systematically robbed them of all valuables. The women and children were ordered to leave towards an adjacent village, and also 65 Kosovo Albanians were killed when fire was opened. Do you know anything about these allegations?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: These allegations are not correct, as I already said at the outset when we were looking at the map of Bela Crkva; our units were outside the village. That is to say it passed through the village without any problems whatsoever and there was no one to do any such thing. There weren't any soldiers or units of the military in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: During the NATO aggression in Kosovo and Metohija or, rather, the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, were you aware of any incident like that, namely that our army and police attacked civilians or committed any crimes against civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I'm not aware of any such thing and I have not even heard of such crimes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, you indicated where you were and where you moved in that part of the territory of Kosovo and Metohija. In paragraph 55 here, it is alleged that our forces deliberately and in a widespread and systematic manner expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Albanians from their homes across the entire province, using threats of force and acts of violence. Please, you commanded a company: Did the army engage in threats and any kind of force against citizens of Albanian ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I'm sure that my unit never did any such thing, nor have I heard of any unit under General Delic's command having done anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you expel anyone?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: A few moments ago you said that you shelled certain firing points, and you said that you only shelled those firing points that constituted a military target, from where firing came from. Please, in paragraph 56 it says that throughout Kosovo the forces of FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and systematic campaign of destruction of property and that they were burning down homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments, et cetera. Please, did you shell towns and villages and destroy civilian targets?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. I never engaged in such shelling or did I ever receive orders to target civilian property or citizens in Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. Do you know anything about the units of the army of Yugoslavia escorting civilians to the border? You were near the border, weren't you? Do you have any knowledge about that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: My unit, the unit I commanded, never escorted the civilian population as it moved towards Albania nor was I given that kind of assignment. My basic assignment was not what is mentioned but the defence of the territory; protection from NATO Air Force attacks and protection of the territory.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Captain, how did you keep up your communication with the superior command? Did you have meetings with your superior officers?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Every day I had meetings in the evening with my battalion commander, and in addition to that, I had wire communication and radio communication.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At these meetings of yours did you hear at any time any information about crimes being committed against civilians or that somebody's property was being destroyed or that a town or village was being shelled?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. During these briefings I never heard of any such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you have specific information as to what was going on in the terrain throughout the zone where you were moving?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did have information, and I reported about all of that to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Briefly describe what happened in the terrain where you were moving about.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the terrain where I was moving about, my basic task was the struggle against Siptar terrorist forces, the protection of the state border, and the protection of the territory of the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia, and the protection of my own personnel, my own unit, and defence from NATO airstrikes while we were completing our task.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you in your units have any contacts with civilians?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, because I was deployed outside the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could your soldiers arbitrarily go into the village and do something impermissible without you knowing about that?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: They could not do it and they wouldn't dare to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any such thing ever happen?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: In my unit, no such thing ever happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let us just deal with one more thing. The seizure of documents of Albanians is referred to often here. You were near the border. Do you know anything about documents being taken away from Albanian inhabitants of Kosovo and Metohija?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't know anything about that. What I know for sure is that my unit did not take away anybody's documents nor did I hear of any unit taking away the documents of a civilian population. I was near the Vrbnica border crossing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you remember -- do you have any idea how many shells you fired during the course of the war throughout these combat activities, roughly?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot recall because it's been quite a while now. It's been six years since the war ended, and the exact information is contained in archives, because every day, when completing our tasks, we submitted reports to the superior command about the materiel used.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. But do you have a rough idea of how many shells you fired?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: One or two 82-millimetre shells were used for engaging military targets, firing points.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: How often did you engage in this kind of activity?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the Orahovac-Suva Reka area, I fought the Siptar terrorist forces at Opterusa, two or three targets at Trljiste, a fortified point from which they were firing at our positions. So that's about four or five times that I opened fire.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was this always only at firing points from which gunfire was coming?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Only.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Captain. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Captain, can I ask you, when was it you retired from the army?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] On the 3rd of March, 2004.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Who was your commander?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: My battalion commander was Lieutenant Colonel Uros Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: Could the witness's other microphone please be turned on. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please have the witness's microphone turned on.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you left on the -- on the evening of the 24th of March, is that right, on deployment?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I set out from Prizren in the direction of Orahovac, and I was staying with my unit in Brnjaca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we can see Brnjaca on a map which we'll return to in a second, but tell us this, please: As a company commander, what records did you keep of what you were doing on that particular evening or night?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: As company commander, I do not keep any written records about what I do with my unit, because I was the leader of a platoon. That was my role when carrying out these particular tasks.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you keep no written records. You reported back to your commander, is that right, Nikolic, what you were doing?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: When carrying out this task, I reported to Zoran Djokic. And as for my own unit, I reported to Uros Nikolic, Lieutenant Colonel Uros Nikolic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So that either Djokic or Nikolic may have contemporaneous records of what you were instructed to do and what you reported on having done; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I report to them orally. I don't know. My commander writes things down in his own notebook, and he probably does have some traces of what I said about what I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you make any report to the VJ Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY, any statement to that commission?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Or to something called the Expert Committee or Expert Commission?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a platoon commander or company commander, you've used platoon and you've used company, so I'll let you decide which, did you have a map showing what you were to do and recording what you had done?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: On the basis of the map of the battalion commander, I worked and reported.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you -- did you carry a map with you, marking on it what you were doing and when and where?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I only have the map when I worked as company commander about the deployment of the units on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, does that apply to what you say was happening when you were at Brnjaca outside Bela Crkva? Is there a map showing or was there a map showing your location there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: First of all, I did not have any positions in Brnjaca. My unit, under the command of Lieutenant Colonel Djokic, came there to carry out an assignment and to rest and prepare for carrying out an assignment which was to take place on the 25th, and this was based on my commander's orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is there a map showing that? Just yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: On this map of Bela Crkva we can see where Brnjaca is. That is where I deployed my unit, in a basement. That's where the unit was. And when I was near Velika Hoca and Opterusa, the positions of the mortars can be seen too.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, we're just concerned with Bela Crkva at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The map you were looking at, Your Honours, it wasn't actually identified properly for the purposes of the record. It's a Delic exhibit, so that's exhibit whatever it is, 300 or -- it's tab 360 of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: When did you first see this map?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I saw this map at the commander of my combat group, but with the total combat deployment of forces on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. I mean you -- it's very helpful. And this particular map, let's just get it on the overhead projector, shall we, so we can look at it. And I want you to take your time with it. Tell me again, you saw it at the commander of your combat group. Where was -- where was it that you saw it; before the operation, during the operation, or after?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Only Bela Crkva, this map?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, this map.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is the first time -- the first time I saw this was during the preparations, but the commander had a map for carrying out the assignment itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's focus on this map. The first time you saw this map was during preparations for what?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: For my testimony.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you discover about who'd written or drawn this map?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: When I got the map, I didn't ask who it was that drew it. I know that commanders made decisions, and then they made the appropriate markings on maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did you understand this to be a map that related to the operation that you'd been on, or what did you understand this map to be? You've been asked questions about it. What's your understanding of what that map is, please?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This map is Bela Crkva and Combat Group 2 deployed to carry out Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. its assignment. Combat Group 2 at the initial line, and the units that were moving towards Orahovac were deployed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What did you understand the map to be? Who prepared it, when, and all that sort thing? It's got a date on it, but what did understand this map to be?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: A map or document, a written document that had to do with the execution of the task involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Prepared at the time or prepared subsequently? That's what I want you to help us with, please.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: The map was made before the task was carried out.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This particular map?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And this is the sort of map, is it, that you as a company or platoon commander saw in your commander's headquarters? Is that right?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Commander of the combat group, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, because -- I mean, they're very conveniently sized, these maps. Maybe they're the sort of maps that commanders would take with them in their small units. Is this the sort of size of map that was made available to you to take with you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is not the size of the map that is otherwise carried around. This is made smaller.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: But it's the sort of map, or the map, whichever you tell us it is, that you saw before the operation?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, let's just look at it and then we'll look at an aerial view. Just tell us, how far is Brnjaca --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm certainly confused. I understood the witness to have said that he saw this for the first time during the preparations to give evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes, but he also, unless I misunderstood it, he also said --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: There are two maps.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The map was made before the task was carried out, and I said, This particular map? and he said Yes. Page 21, lines 4 and 5.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: So that is a map for the operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This particular map is what we're looking at.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help us, please, if you will: What's the distance from Brnjaca to the centre of Bela Crkva?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, yes.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Nice is confusing the witness. Please. The witness said that he saw this map during the preparations, and when he says whether this is a concrete map, the witness understood this to mean whether it is the map of a concrete terrain, not whether this is the map that he was shown during preparations. It's so obvious.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's certainly not obvious to me. And it's not the questions that are confusing, it's the answers, as far as I can tell.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I must press on because obviously with the limited time of the examination-in-chief, I must be brief.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just give us an idea, please, of the distance from Brnjaca to -- from Brnjaca to the centre of Bela Crkva. You can see the grid squares. We haven't got the scale marked on this particular map, so you just tell us, you know the area: How far?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: About 1.000 metres, as the crow flies.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Each of these squares you would say is 500 metres; is that right? We can no doubt check it elsewhere, but just you tell us.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: One centimetre on this map denotes 250 metres in actual fact. So about three or four centimetres. Up to 1.000 metres.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look at this picture, which comes from Exhibit 157, tab 2. On the overhead projector, please. Do you recognise this? This is Bela Crkva. If you want to orientate yourself, I think you can see the mosque pretty well in the middle. Slightly to the right but pretty well in the middle. Do you recognise this as Bela Crkva? You don't recognise it or you do? You're a military man, terrain --

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I cannot recognise it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Because I wanted you to tell us if you could, but if you can't, it doesn't matter, in which direction and at what distance, viewed from this area, you were located on the night of the 24th/25th. This is the centre of Bela Crkva, so it's at least half a kilometre and probably a kilometre away from here that you were based, is it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I can't show you on this map, but I can show you on a map where I was quartered together with my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, you've shown us on this map. You've shown us where Brnjaca is. Tell me --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just leave that map on, please, Usher, if you would be so good. Could you leave the aerial on. I just don't have enough time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you recognise the streambed there that you've been asked about by the accused? He asked you about a streambed. Do you see it there?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No, I don't see it here. Is it in the village?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... help us. We need your assistance. Maybe I can help you. If you -- if you look at the map, on the right-hand side you'll see a line of trees or bushes, wiggling it's way up to the top of the map. Now, do you think that, with all your military experience, might be a streambed? Do you think that might be a streambed? Have a look at it. Hmm? I mean, it could be a hedge, or I suppose it could be a covered road taking a particularly wiggly route, or it could be a streambed. What do you think it is?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I'm an infantry officer, retired currently, and I don't normally deal with aerial pictures. I walk on the ground. This can be a streambed, whereas the Belaja river does have its source in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, if you look towards the top of the village - and just to orientate you if you don't remember, this will be on the way to Rogovo -- Rogova - you'll see a line crossing it which is the railway line, and at the railway line and the streambed, there's a bridge. Do you know that bridge?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You see, it's that bridge, on the evidence from many survivors and eyewitnesses, that people were massacred on the morning of the 25th. You were nowhere near that point, were you? You were a kilometre or a couple of kilometres away. Weren't you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: In an earlier answer, I told you literally that my unit did not execute such tasks. I was near Brnjaca, but it was peaceful, and I didn't hear about any other unit doing such a thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In terms of being disturbed on the morning of the 25th, what was it disturbed you? Because the evidence is to the effect that Bela Crkva was occupied from earlier than the time you say you left, from about 3.00 and 4.00 in the morning. Was it occupation of Bela Crkva that disturbed you?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I said that during the night, around 2400 hours, we were disturbed by the overflying NATO aviation. Nothing else disturbed us. On the 25th in the morning, I raised my unit after the preparations and we set off towards Velika Hoca.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: A few last questions in the time available. Have a look at this similar but slightly more detailed photograph, aerial photograph of Bela Crkva, taken in June of 1999. You see all the damage to the houses? Can you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, it's probably due to NATO airstrikes on the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. What, selectively picking off houses and burning them from the bottom up so that their roofs disappear; is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I did not say that the NATO burned them. I said they shelled and fired in those places. I can enumerate the places where there were NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just looking at that photograph -- actually, have a look at this one, as an infantry officer. Perhaps you will. It's all from the same exhibit. This is even closer still. See the sort of damage to the houses where the walls are standing but the tops are gone, the roofs are gone? You can't see any bomb crater or blast damage. You're saying this is the sort of damage that a bomb caused, or is this the sort of damage caused by artillery destroying a village? Which is it? It's the latter, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: What you are doing now, Mr. Nice, is making statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm asking you a question. You tell us, please. Are you really saying that this is consistent with bomb damage, or is this consistent and only consistent with artillery damage?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: This is probably due to NATO airstrikes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Tell me, what was your function on the following day, the 25th? Were you there going on -- were you out to cleanse villages?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: My task was to support other forces in the breaking up and destruction of Siptar terrorist forces in the direction of Velika Hoca, Opterusa, Samodreza, and Trljiste; that is, to support other forces in the role of the commander of firing mortar unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Were you engaged in cleansing villages? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: No. No. No cleansing of villages but fight against Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: It would be quite wrong to describe what you were doing as cleansing a village, wouldn't it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Mopping up of villages does exist as a tactical activity in a populated area, but support of other forces in fighting Siptar terrorist forces, which was my task, and as such I was active in Trljiste, Opterusa, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Cleansing" was not the word appropriate to the activity you were engaged in on the 25th on your own account, was it?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I told you a moment ago, mopping up exists as a tactical action by infantry forces when you want to break up and destroy the enemy, in this case the Siptar terrorist forces, during combat in a populated area.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You were a witness, weren't you, at a trial involving somebody called Mancic?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Kosovo Albanian shot by whom, a member of your unit?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was not concerned with that part, and I know nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, what was the trial of Mancic about, then?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: It was the trial of Mancic, but I was not a witness called for that particular part that you are mentioning.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... then. Mancic was charged because he told some of his soldiers to shoot Albanians. Correct or incorrect?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: I cannot tell anything about somebody who is not my superior or my commanding officer.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've been asked to give the most broad and general answers about whether anything happened in Kosovo. Last time I'll give you a chance: Was Mancic charged with causing -- or instructing his soldiers to shoot Albanians? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: He was convicted.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Any re-examination, Mr. Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one question, Captain, if you can answer it based on your experience and your knowledge. If we're talking about consequences of a shell fired from an anti -- sorry, from an airborne gun versus the consequences of a shell fired from a ground-based gun, can we distinguish between the two?

utterances.speaker: HUSEIN SARVANOVIC
utterances.text: We can distinguish between various effects of the shell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Captain, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for attending at the Tribunal to give it. You may now leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: The next witness, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My next witness is Lieutenant Colonel Zlatko Odak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, it is Mr. Janos Sel who is outside - there is some confusion - not Lieutenant Colonel Odak. So why don't we just proceed with Mr. Janos Sel. Let Mr. Janos Sel be brought in. What's his status, Mr. Milosevic, Mr. Sel? Is he an army officer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes; lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Well, we're back to the original schedule. It's Mr. Odak. Let Mr. Odak be brought in. Perhaps the court deputy will take in consideration that all these witnesses today are short witnesses, and so the witnesses who are to be called should be alerted to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let the witness make the declaration.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You may sit. Mr. Milosevic, you may begin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Lieutenant Colonel.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Would you please introduce yourself as briefly as you can.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: My name is Zlatko Odak. I was born on the 8th of May, 1971, in Belgrade. I am Serb by ethnicity. I graduated from the military high school, Military Academy of the Ground Forces, and the advanced training school for staffs in headquarters. I occupied various positions from commander of rifle platoon to chief of staff of a brigade. That would be the briefest I could make it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where did you serve?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: From 1986, when I finished the military academy, I served in the Djakovica garrison until 1999 when we pulled out of Kosovo. And later --

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, go on.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Later in garrisons in Belgrade and in Kragujevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That would make you one of the few officers in the army of Yugoslavia, and before that the Yugoslav People's Army, who had spent 15 years in the Djakovica garrison -- almost 15 years?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: To be exact, 13 and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I suppose you know very well the circumstances, the situation, the conditions in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, I know all about that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Are you now a serving officer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Robinson. My current rank is lieutenant colonel.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where were you during the war in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: During the war in Kosovo, I occupied two positions, practically. I was commander of the Logistics Battalion in Air Defence Brigade at the beginning of the war. That was the 52nd PVO Brigade. And I later asked to be transferred back to the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade, and that's where I served the second half of the war, as deputy commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Up to the middle of the war you say; what would that be precisely?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, I don't remember the exact date, but it was around the 20th May, something like that. Until then I was in the 52nd Brigade, and then I moved to the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So until the 20th May you were commander of the logistics battalion of this 52nd Anti-aircraft Defence Brigade in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Correct. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Until approximately the 20th of May. Now, tell me, please, Lieutenant Colonel, your battalion was stationed in Djakovica all of the time. Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any other unit stationed in Djakovica at the same time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In the town of Djakovica itself, there was only the command artillery battalion. No other units were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So apart from the command of your brigade, you were the only unit in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: We have heard various references here to various crimes committed in Djakovica, allegedly committed by FRY forces. That's why I want to ask you again: Only your unit was in Djakovica at the time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, plus the command battalion that caters to the command of the brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, but tell me very briefly, what was the situation in Djakovica, since you lived there 14 years? What was the situation there as long as you lived there? Did you have social bonds, friends? Did you socialise with Albanians, for instance? They are numerous in Djakovica. Quite simply, what was life like in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I actually got married in Djakovica. My father-in-law and generally my wife's family grew up together with Albanians, and through them I came to know a lot of Albanians and I socialised with them just as I socialised with Serbs and members of all other ethnicities.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did any problems arise due to different ethnicities?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When did the first problems begin to occur? Because as somebody who lived there for more than a decade and a half, you could tell us that.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, the first problems started to appear elsewhere in Kosovo, not exactly in Djakovica at first. In 1979, there were unrests, and until 1997, 1998, there were no major unrests.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What exactly happened in 1998 and 1999 prior to the beginning of the war? What was going on?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In 1998, I was commander of Combat Group 2 of the 549th Brigade, and I got a task to provide in-depth protection for the state border in the broader area of the Mitar Vojinovic watchtower. That is the area overlooking Popovac village and another village, Babaj Boks, somewhere halfway between the watchtower and the state border. We were given this task because smuggling of weapons across the border was an increasingly frequent occurrence. So our combat group secured this area all the way until September 1998. In this period, from Smonica village and Popovac village there would be several attacks per day on vehicles that supplied the watchtower personnel, and my job was to provide security on these routes used by our personnel to reach Kosare, Kosare, Molina, the watchtower, et cetera. In the course of execution of these tasks, I also captured six terrorists somewhere above Popovac village. I think it was in early May.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mean May 1998?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: It was actually end May. I captured six terrorists who were turned over to the authorities. In this period, there were unrelenting attacks by terrorists from Smonica, Bezanic, and other villages. Kvetz [phoen] village as well, injuring many soldiers. In early August I received an order to attack terrorists in Kvetz and Smonica villages, which I did. And in one of our actions, they were defeated in the course of one day and withdrew towards Racaj village. Several days later, I mounted an attack -- or, rather, I went into pursuit of the terrorists. However, they hid in the woods in this area, which is a very inhospitable terrain. That area was important to them because of the proximity of the state border, and they kept a constant presence in that area. Seremete, Koc [phoen], Racaj, et cetera, so that they could transfer arms across the state border deep into the territory of Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: At the same time you were providing security on a road?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, Djakovica-Ponosevac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And why was that communication line or road important for us or, rather, you, given this assignment to provide security for it, and why was it important to the Siptar terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, it was important to us because it was the supply route for the Morina, Kosare and other watchtowers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So these watchtowers were supplied by that supply route?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes. And at one point the terrorists blocked off that communication line, cut it off, and for the terrorists it was an important communication line because it was close to the border. And in fact, they were trying continuously, as they did in 1998 and 1999, to join up their forces or join up the territory with Albania, that territory with Albania, so that they would be able to bring in weapons along that route. That would be the easiest way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We will adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Have we lost the witness? Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sometime in May 1998 when you went into anti-terrorist action, you captured six terrorists.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us of the circumstances and where that was exactly.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, during that period the terrorists had blocked off the road towards the Morina watchtowers and Kosare watchtower and cut off the supply route to our units, and so I was given the task of providing security for lateral movement of the unit to lift the blockade and to make it possible for supplies to come in to the watchtowers on that supply route. Above the village of Popovac itself I came across a group of terrorists who had set up an ambush and were preparing to attack the column. That's just one part of the terrorists who were in Popovac. And I captured them. Then they attacked the column that was moving. And since we started heavy pursuit of them, they went off in the area of the village of Smonica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, and what were the proceedings, steps taken with those you captured?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The people we captured we took to the camp and then handed them over to the MUP forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did anybody abuse them in any way, mistreat them?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You said a moment ago something about what was happening along that Djakovica-Ponosevac communication line, along that road, and the surrounding villages, the villages that you enumerated where the terrorist groups were located that you engaged with. Now, what happened in the town of Djakovica itself? Was there any violence there, any incidents of any kind?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: You mean during the war?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No, I mean at that time in 1998 and before the war actually broke out.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, no, there were no incidents in the town itself. People lived normally. There were no untoward events happening. The terrorists otherwise avoided large towns because they found their strongholds in the villages where they actually forced the population to help them, to join up with them, and they felt safest and most secure there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On many occasions here we had saw -- well, I'm not going to ask you to indicate on the map because this was pointed out a number of times, but you had your area of responsibility in the region of Djakovica itself and the town of Djakovica itself; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, that general area of Djakovica, how was it significant as an entire region? Was it significant for the terrorist forces in any way?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, I said a moment ago that it was one of the most important regions, and this was seen later on during the war, because there were constant attacks launched on the -- our forces along the border belt, and from the Republic of Albania as well as from our territory in-depth. They tried to link up the terrain with Albania and thus create grounds for the easier transport of terrorist forces from the Republic of Albania into Kosovo and Metohija.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Where was the most intense concentration of terrorist forces?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, the villages I've already mentioned; Nec, Smonica, Bezanici, Racaj, Pacaj, Dolosaj, Seremete, Meja. It was a circle or circular territory which is fairly heavily forested and allows for terrorists to hide there. So they used that general area quite a lot, both in 1998 and 1999 as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's move on to 1999 now, please. In paragraph 63 of the indictment, 63(h), in fact, it says that by March, and we're talking about 1999, the number of inhabitants in the town of Djakovica significantly increased because of a large number of internally displaced persons who fled their villages to escape deliberate shelling, deliberate shelling by forces of the FRY and Serbia during 1998, and to escape the armed conflict between these forces and members of the Kosovo Liberation Army, the so-called Liberation Army. Now, as you yourself were present in Djakovica itself, what can you say about those allegations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, first of all, there was no, to use the term that is used there, shelling. There was no shelling, I don't know of this term as part of military terminology. I don't know of any shelling. What the army did was to target targets where the terrorists were firing from, facilities, features, bunkers, and any other points, firing points, terrorist firing points. There was no deliberate shelling.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what about this large concentration of population in Djakovica by March 1999? You have been living in Djakovica yourself for a decade and a half. What can you tell us about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, all I can say is to explain it through the way in which the terrorists acted, if I may be allowed to do so. The terrorists acted in the following manner: They would arrive in a village, they would effect forceful mobilisation, force the population to mobilise, force the population to purchase weapons, usually rifles which cost between 200 to 300 German marks - that was the going price - then they would order the population to fortify, to dig trenches around the villages, and by doing so they created the impression that the village was defending itself. And the army -- or, rather when, the army did not attack, the population was in the village, of course, and then the next form of action was that the terrorists attacked the army or the internal affairs forces. When the army retaliates, the terrorists order the population to leave the village, creating the impression in that way that the population had moved out under pressure from the army, whereas what was actually happening was quite the reverse. And I was a personal witness of this. Wherever we attacked a village, the population moved out of those villages in the course of action because the terrorists forced them to flee, to leave their villages.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Furthermore, it states that the continual movement of these internally displaced persons increased after the 24th of March, 1999, when, as it says here in the indictment, following violent expulsions - violent expulsions, mark you - in the town of Djakovica, many internally displaced persons returned from the town of Djakovica to the outlying villages only to be expelled from these villages again by forces of the FRY and Serbia. Now, you were in Djakovica yourself. What kind of violent expulsion was this?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: There was no violent expulsion, not only in the town of Djakovica but nowhere in the region that I was in, nor did I ever hear there were incidents of violent expulsions. And I told you how the terrorists acted. I described that, how they made the population move out and how they displaced the population, et cetera. And what I do know for certain is that the population fled from the NATO bombing. And when I talked to the people personally, to refugees, I talked to them, they said they had taken refuge with relatives in the internal regions of the country where they thought they would be safer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then it says that the Serb forces controlled and coordinated the movement of these internally displaced persons as they travelled from these villages to and from the town of Djakovica and finally to the border between Kosovo and the Republic of Albania. Persons travelling on foot were sent from the town of Djakovica directly toward one of several border crossings. Persons travelling in motor vehicles were routed first towards the town of Prizren before approaching the border and crossing. Tell us, please, did the army control the refugee movements and what is true in these allegations?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The army did not control the movement of refugees nor was it assigned that task. Its prime assignment, the prime assignment of the army was to defend the country from the NATO aggression. Since I was in the town of Djakovica myself, I, unfortunately, saw that population, those inhabitants, and I had a chance of talking to the people who were moving, on the move. From Mitrovica there were a lot of children among them. They were terrible images to behold. And I had occasion to talk to these people, and principally they were afraid of the bombing. And secondly, many of them claimed that the terrorists had threatened them and that they were told that they had to go to Albania and were not allowed to go back home, probably to create the impression of an alleged humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 63(i), it says that from on or about the 24th of March, which was the first day of the war, through the 11th of May -- you were there until the 20th of May in Djakovica, were you not?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So this covers this entire period that you were there; is that right? Anyway, it says from on or about the 24th of March through the 11th of May, forces of the FRY and Serbia began forcing residents of the town of Djakovica to leave, and these forces spread out through the town and went from house to house, ordering Kosovo Albanians from their homes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That is absolutely not correct. I and my unit were in Djakovica, and I communicated with the population of Djakovica all the time, so that those facts are certainly not correct ones. I don't know what else you -- I can say on that point. Where my unit was, the population lived in Djakovica normally, those who were not afraid of the bombing, of course, and who remained, who stayed on where they were. Or they didn't have anywhere to go, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, do you know anything about our forces going from house to house, ordering and forcing the population to leave their homes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Once again, I state that my unit was there, and my unit had the task of ensuring supplies, the various health supplies and food and anything else, and it's not true that that's what that they engaged in.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Then they go on to state in that same paragraph that many were killed and many were threatened with death and that many properties belonging to Kosovo Albanians were set fire to where the properties and shops of Serbs were protected. So that is the general image that is portrayed here. Is it true? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, it's not correct that anybody was threatened nor that people were expulsed nor was the property of Albanians set fire to. What was -- what resulted in properties being set fire to was the result of NATO bombings. And my battalion was in the northern parts of Djakovica, towards Pec, the area towards Pec, where the population lived. The population of Djakovica lived in that area, of course, and there were strikes at my unit many times. So that many facilities, civilian facilities, were hit during those strikes. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since you were there yourself, did you personally tour all these areas that were targeted; and what did you see if you did?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, I was there. My unit was on an assignment throughout the town. I went into town myself frequently to tour the town. And what sprang to the eye, what was most evident as you exit Djakovica was the column of refugees that was hit. I think it was on the 24th, in actual fact. 24th of April. I'm not quite sure of the date. Anyway, the refugees were hit by the NATO bombs. As well always the Maja settlement, where there were Serb refugees from Krajina. Another thing that was hit was the factory of Erenik Sokara, which is an area predominantly populated by the Serbs, and a number of people were killed when the factory was bombed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Sokara. It says "Sokora" here, but it's Sokara. You mean the juice producing factory, fruit juice producing factory, and that's how you refer to it in the local jargon?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes. And specifically targeted was area bordering on Mount Cabrat, that part of town. And as far as I know, the mosque was destroyed there and that part was burnt as a result of the NATO bombings, because at Mount Cabrat was the positions of the rocket divisions until they dislocated to other areas. They would move quite frequently, but that's where their positions used to be, and they put models up there which were constantly targeted by NATO. So these targets would be missed and civilian targets would be hit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, since you were in command of practically the only unit that was in Djakovica, do you know whether any one of your soldiers set fire to any houses, for example?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, what I can tell you is that certainly was not done, at least to the best of my knowledge. And I was considered to be a very strict officer myself. My brigade commander, Djosan, who was a colonel at the time, was also a commanding officer who would not allow anything like that to happen, and any cases of criminality, crimes of any kind, steps were taken to prosecute.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It says here in this paragraph, in paragraph 63, that on the 24th of March, 1999, the old mosque at Rogovo, the old mosque in Rogovo, then the bazaar, the Hadun [as interpreted] mosque and the adjoining Islamic library "were among the several cultural sites substantially and/or totally destroyed." What do you know about that? You were there, on the spot.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: As to the mosque in Rogovo, I can't say one way or another. I wasn't there during that period of time. However, I mentioned a moment ago that that particular mosque was adjoining the Cabrat area. Are you referring to the Hadum Mosque?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, Hadum. All right, very well.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: So that part bordering on Cabrat hill was frequently targeted -- not frequently but daily targeted by NATO in the NATO strikes. So that part of town was the part of town that was destroyed most, and that's where that library was hit and -- the Islamic library -- the mosque and the library.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm not asking you about where you were not, but the Hadum Mosque, the bazaar, the Hadum library. Tell us about the bazaar. What was that all about? What is the bazaar in Djakovica? It's a marketplace, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, it's a marketplace if we're thinking of the same thing, the same mosque.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: No. The mosque is one thing, the Hadum mosque is one thing, but the bazaar in Djakovica, what is that? Is it a centre or what?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The bazaar. The bazaar, yes, I'm sorry, yes, I see. The bazaar is located, well, near the centre of town.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And how was that destroyed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Near the bazaar mosque was where my unit was, part of my unit, and it was that unit that was targeted. I can't tell you the exact day that this happened, but it was hit by a NATO bomb.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, the -- during the period from the 2nd to the 4th of April, it says here thousands of Kosovo Albanians living in the town of Djakovica and neighbouring villages joined a large convoy, either on foot or driving in cars, trucks, and tractors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Let me just ask the lieutenant colonel this: You're saying, then, that it was a NATO bomb that destroyed the bazaar?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: I mean, how do you know this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, as I said, my unit was located -- since the areas of deployment were changed frequently, at one time it was close to the bazaar mosque, and areas were targeted frequently, the areas that my unit was deployed in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And so you witnessed the bombing of the bazaar by NATO, NATO planes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, not at that point in time, at exactly that moment, but the testimony of my soldiers and those who were there right then. I came later on. I don't remember exactly when that was. Perhaps a half an hour later, an hour later. But anyway, wherever my unit was targeted, I would turn up soon afterwards once they reported back to me about what had happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: You say you don't remember the date, but do you remember the day of the week when this took place?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm really sorry, Mr. Robinson. Six years have gone by since then. I really can't remember just now. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: And was -- what else was destroyed, if anything, by the NATO bombs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I mentioned this a moment ago: Part of Djakovica, the part bordering on the hill called Cabrat, above Djakovica. And that was almost completely destroyed by the bombing, that area. And I say again that that's where the firepower positions were and where we had put up models. And there were daily NATO strikes in that area, targeting that. And another -- or civilian facilities around the barracks were completely destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In the area of the bazaar, was anything else destroyed by NATO bombing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, the surrounding houses were destroyed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I asked you in relation to this allegation that between the 2nd and the 4th of Albanians [as interpreted] thousands of Kosovo Albanians living in the town of Djakovica and neighbouring villages joined a large convoy, either on foot, or driving in cars, tractors and trucks, and moved to the border with Albania. What do you know about this? Why did these people go and was there a massive departure from Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I've said a few moments ago that some inhabitants of Djakovica left from fear from NATO bombings and others under threats of the terrorists that they had to leave their villages and go to Albania. They went where they thought they'd be safe. Some went to Albania. Others stayed with their relatives in Djakovica. Others were staying in Raca, Moglica, Petrusa, and other villages. So there was no expulsion. They went where they thought they were safer.
