utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, what would be the basis for your conclusion that some of the inhabitants left from fear for NATO bombing? What precise information do you have in this regard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've already said in response to the previous question: I directly spoke to people who were in the convoy of refugees, a group of refugees, about 100 of them, women, men, children, old people. Since they were passing by the Emin Duraku factory, they were coming from the direction of Kosovska Mitrovica and Pec where my command was in that factory. My command was in that factory. And at one moment that hill of Cabrat was bombed. It's about 3 to 400 metres away from the road where the column of refugees was. I received them in the compound of the factory. We gave them food, water, whatever we had. And some people were complaining there about the situation. They said they were afraid of the bombing, that they had to go to Albania. Others were saying other things. But again, they were afraid that someone might overhear what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's just clarify another detail: What about the population of the town itself? Were they leaving en masse? You said that some went to stay in villages and some went to stay with relatives in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, they were not moving out en masse. That became obvious at the end of the war. Djakovica's population had doubled, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as a rule, citizens were not leaving the town of Djakovica itself?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Further on, it says that the forces of FRY and Serbia directed those fleeing along pre-arranged routes and at checkpoints along the way most Kosovo Albanians had their identification papers and licence plates seized. In some instances, Yugoslav army trucks were used to transport persons to the border with Albania. What do you say about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, as I've already said, the army did not control the movement of civilians. All units were at the state border, where they were deployed in order to organise the defence. I did not hear of anyone exercising control there, taking IDs, taking them in vehicles to the border. Those poor people who had vehicles went in those vehicles and others even walked. So I certainly would have heard had something like that happened, because I was in Djakovica non-stop. In town, that is.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In paragraph 63(ii), it says that in the early morning hours on the 27th of April --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The accused is making the same mistake that he makes about citing paragraphs of the indictment, and it's only corrected for the purposes of the record. In each case it's 63(h)(i) or (ii), and it would help if we got that right when he cites from the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Please bear that in mind, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In the early morning hours of the 27th of April, 1999, or around that time, the forces of the FRY and Serbia launched a massive attack against the Carragojs, Erenik, and Trava valleys, Djakovica municipality, in order to drive the population out of the area. What do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I've already said in response to the previous questions that this region was very important for the terrorists. Their concentration in that area varied all the time. Their numbers varied. At one point, according to the information I had, they jeopardised the rear of our units or, rather, of the fighting echelons of the units. So it was necessary to search the area and to make it impossible for the terrorists to jeopardise our units. As far as I know, the only goal of that action was to expel the terrorists from that region.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I quoted exactly. All of Djakovica is in 63(h), and this is subparagraph (ii).

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's like Roman 2. But let us proceed.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it looks like an i. There's a dot on top.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could Mr. Milosevic's microphone please be adjusted. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Would you see that the microphone for the accused is adjusted. There is a request from the interpreter. Yes, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In this paragraph that I mentioned to you a few moments ago, in Meja, Korenica and Meja-Orize, a large number of civilians were separated from the mass of fleeing villagers, and they were abducted and executed. Further on, it says that this went on throughout the entire day. Villagers under direct threat from the forces of the FRY and Serbia left their homes and joined several convoys of refugees using tractors, horse carts, and cars, and eventually crossed into Albania. And then again that many had their identity documents confiscated before they crossed the border. So what do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: You mean the 27th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, the 27th of April. That's this entire subparagraph. I told you, the 27th of April. This major offensive, as it is called here, and then what I quoted to you, that in these villages a large number, as yet undetermined, of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated from the mass of fleeing civilians, abducted and executed.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't have any information that something like that happened - I would have to know because part of my unit took part in that action, in the blockade of that area - the order of the brigade commander, because there weren't any other units in Djakovica, and there wasn't a unit that would intervene in case the terrorists attacked the town itself. I was given orders to establish a company about 100 men strong, that is to say three platoons, that one intervene if the terrorists attacked, or they would go on any mission as assigned by the corps command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So as commander of the logistics battalion, you don't really have any combat function in this.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. The battalion, simply because there weren't any other units there, I singled out some soldiers and formed the unit of these men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead. Please finish.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I took part in this action, and I don't have any information to the effect that something like that happened. I would have had to hear about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In which capacity did you take part in that action?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Since I am an infantry officer, I commanded this company, and my task was to take the blockade line above the village of Osek Hilja and Skivjane.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now I'm just going to ask you to show that on the overhead projector. I hope that you have this map in tab 2. Unfortunately, I haven't got it here. Have you got the exhibits there? This is a map of Meja. D321, tab 29.1.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: My unit was at the blockade line. Trig 468. Trig 460. Have you seen it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Yes, yes. And what is the length of the line of blockade that you held with your unit?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, it's about a kilometre and a half. A kilometre or a kilometre and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. You held a line of blockade that was at least one kilometre long.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As you held this blockade line, did you see any of what is alleged here, anything that is alleged here?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: This is an area that is highly forested. This is near Osek Hilja and Skivjane. It's very hard to see there. And when the blockade line was taken, part of my unit went a -- a bit further up and saw terrorists at the entrance of the village of Racaj. As a matter of fact, they even found a shelter there where they were staying, and the terrorists left, went back to the village, and our exclusive task was to prevent any breakthrough through the line of blockade.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So you did not enter the village in order to find the terrorists?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, no, no. We were really not in a position to see anything from the trees and bushes, to see what was going on there. But on the 27th and 28th, gunfire was heard, that is to say fighting with the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. When you set out to carry out that task, I assumed Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. that you received orders as to what your assignment was.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Bear in mind that 66(i) of the indictment says the same thing as in paragraph 63: A massive attack against the Kosovo Albanians, population of Carragojs, Trava and Erenik valleys, in order to drive the population out of the area. That is what is written there. Now, tell me, what was your task? What were your intentions? As commander of this group or this company that you established and that was assigned to block this line of one kilometre or kilometre and a half, what was your task, your intentions, your objectives, what?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The task of that company that was established was to take that line of blockade and to prevent the terrorists from withdrawing to the villages of Racaj, Osek Hilja, and -- and Racaj-Skivjane. And if civilians were to withdraw from the village, then we were supposed to return them to the village. Why should we return them? For one reason only. I already told you in which way the terrorists operated. So as soon as the army attacked, the terrorists ordered the villagers to leave the village. However, I didn't have anyone withdrawing in my area and I didn't really have any contact with the terrorists. I didn't have any fighting with them or anything. So that's how the terrorists operated: They forced the villagers to leave the village, and in this way they were pretending that it was the army that was jeopardising the population. The only objective was -- the only objective of that action was to defeat the terrorists. They kept returning there all the time from 1998, and they were threatening our units in-depth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You were battalion commander. You received orders from your brigade commander.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any idea there or order or were any instructions given to you to do anything hostile towards the civilians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Certainly not, not in a single order that I received during the war and while I was in the 52nd Brigade and in the 549th Brigade. There was no such order. And it's certain that we would never do that to our own population nor did we do it then. The only intention was to defeat the terrorists in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. It says here that a large number of members of the forces of FRY and Serbia were used there and that many checkpoints were set up and that villagers were leaving the area all the time under direct threat of the forces of the FRY and Serbia, and they were joining this convoy. Tell us, please, what is correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I told you that the village population was leaving only on orders from the terrorists. "Major forces," what does "major forces" mean? If in an area of a kilometre and a half you have 90 men, these are not major forces. So the other units, too. Whatever they managed to get out of the combat deployment they did in order to be in a position to carry out that particular mission.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The next allegation in the same paragraph is that in Meja, Korenica, Meja-Orize, a large and as yet undetermined number of Kosovo Albanian civilian males were separated from the mass of fleeing villagers and abducted. Many were summarily executed and approximately 300 persons are still missing. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: It's not true that anything like that happened or that I know about it. There are certainly terrorists who got killed. That is a certainty because the whole operation was conducted for that purpose. But as for the civilian population being killed or dying, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I will now question you on a subject different from Meja. In 66(e), the date mentioned is the 26th of March, 1999. When were you -- where were you then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Since you were in Djakovica on that day and for 15 years before that, you can tell me this: It says that forces of FRY and Serbia came to a house at 134A Ymer Grezda Street. The women and children inside the house were separated from the men and were ordered to go upstairs. The forces of the FRY and Serbia then shot and killed the six Kosovo Albanian men who were in the house. So it was the 26th of March.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't know where the street is, but since I was in Djakovica at the time, I would have certainly heard if something like that happened. I have no knowledge of anything similar, and I don't believe it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, on the 26th of March, was there any other unit in Djakovica apart from yours?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So if this were true, then it would have been -- it would have had to be members of your unit involved.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, according to what you say, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible for members of your unit to do something like that without you knowing?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, impossible. I am going to repeat myself, but I have to say that in our army, just like in any other army, there are certain principles we abide by, and certainly somebody would have notified me; either one of the superior officers -- rather, subordinate officers, or one of the soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The smallest unit that was subordinated to you was a platoon, followed by a company.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Could a squad or a platoon independently perform a task that would be some sort of invitation to acting without official leave?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That was impossible. The soldiers were under constant supervision of their superiors, and if the allegation is that this incident happened at night, then it is certain that none of the soldiers went about town at night. It was very strictly prohibited for their own safety, for the safety of personnel. They were not allowed to leave their area of deployment.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was it possible that any of them left their place of deployment without permission?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. We didn't have any such cases.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In 66(h), it says that on the late evening of 1st April, 1999, or about that time, and continuing through the early morning hours of the 2nd of April, 1999, forces of the FRY and Serbia launched an operation against the Qerim district of Djakovica. Over a period of several hours, forces of the FRY and Serbia forcibly entered the houses of Kosovo Albanians in Qerim, killed the occupants, and then set fire to the buildings. So this here is a whole operation taking place at night, in the night of the 1st of April. Where were you then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I was probably on my command post - where else? - within the perimeter of the Emin Duraku factory. But through a combination of circumstances that evening my village [as interpreted] had passed through Ljug Bunar and Qerim. A vehicle was hit there and I got orders to get a fire brigade vehicle and a -- and an ambulance urgently. I asked one of my subordinates in charge of such matters and told him to meet those vehicles outside Djakovica near the bridge on the road leading to Pristina. They left. They performed that task. They transported the bodies of the soldiers who had been killed, lent assistance to the injured, returned to the command. And every time a commander returns from a mission, he informs me about the mission performed and any problems he may have encountered. On that occasion he told me that he had passed through the terrain, it was absolutely peaceful, there were no lights anywhere in the area they had passed through, and they hadn't noticed anything happening. So I don't believe that anything happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, if you remember, the time when this radar was hit upon which you sent that ambulance, the fire brigade vehicle?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't remember exactly. I think it was around midnight. I can't tell you precisely.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So it was right in the middle of this time when purportedly some sort of operation was going on in Qerim?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When the forces of the FRY and Serbia were forcibly entering Kosovo Albanian houses and killing occupants.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, they passed through the area very frequently. I would have noticed, I suppose, if something like that had happened. My subordinate commander, as I told you, informed me that there was nothing going on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: What other forces were there? Who could have been involved?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, that rocket battalion was not exactly there, some way off.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Well, the rocket battalion has its own job. They are a crew to a weapon, and they are --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: They are constantly on the alert, and they are not allowed to leave the weapon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: It also says in the same paragraph that on that occasion dozens of houses were destroyed. So around midnight, when the radar was hit and you sent a rescue team, that is the time when allegedly dozens of homes were destroyed and over 50 persons were killed. For example, it reads: "In a house located at 157 Milos Gilic Street, forces of the FRY and Serbia shot the occupants and then set the house on fire. As a result of the shootings and the fires set by the forces of the FRY and Serbia at that single location, 20 Kosovo Albanians were killed, of whom 19 were women and children."

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, that's absolutely not correct. I would certainly know if anything like that had happened, because as I said, my units passed by at the same time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: That's the same night, between the 1st and the 2nd of April.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In that case, it's not correct that anything like that happened.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: In your operations, was any civilians killed at all, even one?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, in those operations in which I participated, I did not have occasion to see any civilians killed, or even terrorists killed, for that matter. It's possible that a civilian gets killed in an exchange of fire, but we didn't find any bodies of civilians, or even terrorists, as I said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, on more than one occasion you gave statements concerning events in Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Those statements were introduced through General Djosan, who was commander of your brigade.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In these statements that you gave, did you explain precisely what you knew about the subjects you were asked to talk about?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In tab 8 -- I hope you have it in front of you. In tab 8 there is --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: If the accused could give the Djosan exhibit reference then we could be sure we find the right document. It's not that easy to track them down that quickly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, let us have the exhibit number.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Give me just a moment to find it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: D321, tab 8. The list says it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In your set, Mr. Odak, it's in tab 3. Let us just make sure that we're looking at the same document. I have in front of me your statement on the activities of the unit on the 1st of April, on the 27th and 28th of April, and another statement about the activities of your unit separately on the 28th of April. That's three statements made by you to the Commission for Cooperation with the ICTY, to the expert team specifically. Do you have the same statements?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On 1st of April, that is the date when our forces allegedly committed certain crimes over there, you describe what you were doing and what your assignment was. You were at the time commander of the logistics battalion, and you explain in the second paragraph where the battalion was deployed.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Just a second, Mr. Milosevic. All the Chamber has received is a sheet of index which says about the documents we are going to use with this witness, but number 3 says it's D321, tab 8. It says it is the statement of unit engagement on 24th of March. It does not refer to the event of 1st of April. So could you make it clear.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, Mr. Kwon, I'm reading what I have in my set of documents from a statement written by Mr. Odak. It says activities of the unit on the 1st of April, 1999. I'm only reading what's written on his statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's misleading on the index. These are the statements written for the commission, referring to those incidents in 1999.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: So it's the 1st of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's the 1st of April instead of the 24th of March, is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: The incidents refer to the 24th of March. Tab 8 is a document written the 26th of December, 2002, and tab 3 in this index but tab 8 of the Djosan index.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Milosevic has just suggested that there were three statements in the hands of the witness; one relating to the 1st of April, one relating to the 27th and the 28th, and one then relating to the 28th. Now, the only one on the index that he's produced is one relating to the 24th of March, which he hasn't mentioned, and then one relating to the 27th and 28th, which might be one of the three.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It seems that D321, tab 11, has been missed off the index, because that's a statement dated the 26th of December, 2002, referring to the 1st of April, 1999. It was an untranslated document in Djosan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thanks for that clarification, Mr. Kay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Is a statement of that within Djosan tab 11?

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: It's a statement within the Djosan records, by Mr. Odak.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: These are three Odak statements within Djosan.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Kay. Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Bonomy said it correctly. I mentioned three statements that I have in my set of documents, and through the good offices of the liaison officer, I have received the document related to the 24th of March now as well, which is not contained in my set of documents but we can look at that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Let's take a look at the statement dated the 1st of April first, if you have it before you.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I hope you are going to bear in mind what I quoted, that a crime of some sort had been committed in the Qerim settlement.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: This one is not translated. Handling it is problematic when I imagine the accused is going to ask that it be moved into evidence. Perhaps it could go on the overhead projector. It's only just over one page long, and rather than summarise, if there's any part he relies on, Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. perhaps he could quote it so we know exactly what it says.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes. Let be it placed on the -- it's on the ELMO. Mr. Milosevic, is there a particular section that you wish to refer to, bearing in mind that it's not translated.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, this was provided during the testimony of General Djosan, and as you know, considerable time has elapsed since then and it certainly could have been translated.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: But take a look at paragraph 3, now, please, Lieutenant Colonel, and it says on the 1st of April, 1999 - this is important because of the time - it says: "A little before midnight I received an assignment urgently to go to the area of the village of Ljug Bunar which was where the fire positions were of the artillery battalion and radar P15 to send a motor vehicle and anti-fire -- and a fire brigade system truck there." So the radar had been hit, there was burning going on, and you received that assignment soon before midnight; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And your medical corps, a truck, the cistern and everything else -- the truck and everything that was dispatched to assist, how long did it take them to get there?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: They went within the space of 30 to 45 minutes. They were dispatched there, they set off within the space of 30 to 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I see, set off. And how long did it take them to reach the area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: It took them 30 minutes. It's not a long way away, but as it was night-time, that's how long it took them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right, you don't know how long they spent there, but do you know when they returned after putting out -- extinguishing the fire and when the medical corps turned up and so on, ambulance?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, since the time they set off, as far as I remember, they returned two hours later, roughly two hours later.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. And if we were to reconstruct these events, they set off a little after midnight and returned a little after 2.00 a.m., roughly. Can we say that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, we can.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the team, did it have to pass through the Qerim settlement both on its way out and on its way back?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, they had to pass that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And who made up the team?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The team was composed of a squad, an officer with seven soldiers providing security; there was an ambulance with a doctor, a nurse, a medical technician and so forth; and a fire-fighting -- fire-fighting truck.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Right. So that's the assistance you sent out.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Was there any other unit - yours or anybody else's - along that route and in that general area?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Take a look at the penultimate paragraph, the middle of that paragraph on page 1.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: The one that begins: "I quickly effected the preparations ..." et cetera. And in the middle, what does it say: "Upon returning from the assignment ..." You read it out, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: "Upon returning from the assignment, I was informed by the security commander that the road leading to Qerim was empty. When returning from the assignment, I was informed by the security commander that the road up to the village of Ljug Bunar, which leads through the Qerim settlement, was completely empty, that it was dark and they didn't encounter anybody on the way. He also informed me that the killed soldiers were brought to the garrison clinic and that Aleksandar Gajic, Sergeant, and soldier private -- a private who was with him at the radar were transferred to the clinic, but that the radar -" P15 was the radar - "that they were not able to put out the fire on the P15 radar."

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And what does it say in the last paragraph -- or, rather, is that roughly what you told us when I asked you a question about that event between the 1st and 2nd of April?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes. I've already answered that question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. And what does it say in the last paragraph? "As to the alleged crimes committed in the village of Qerim, I heard about them at the end of 2001 for the first time."

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Lieutenant Colonel. Let us just take a look at this second statement that I have, relating to the 27th and 28th of April. I hope that that one has been translated, and if need be, we can place it on the overhead projector. No problem there, I think. We're going to skip over the first part, what you did on so on. Mention is made of what you mentioned a moment ago, that you had established a company within the frameworks of your battalion. And what does it say, that the reason for setting up a unit of this kind was the situation, that is to say that in the town of Djakovica there was not a single combat unit.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And you explained that to us a moment ago. Now, what does it say in the last sentence of this paragraph? It was the task of the unit to intervene where?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In places where the Siptar terrorist forces jeopardised the security of our units in the town and the Pristina Corps command post, the brigade command post, garrison, infirmary, and the local population, in order to operate in coordination with other units in the event of an attack by the Siptar terrorist forces.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And that in principle was the main task, was it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And it says here that you were given the assignment -- "On the 25th of April I was given a task," it says, "for the intervention unit to accomplish in the early hours of the 27th of April, 1999, which was to take the following line for a seal-off operation ..." Trig, the trig you pointed out to us, the trig point. And what does it say in the last line there? Commanders and soldiers. What does it say? "I carried out necessary preparations for the combat operation and I regulated the procedure of units and individuals in the event of encountering Siptar terrorist forces and in the event of evacuating the civilian population over the seal-off-line," or blockade line. In all our orders, in fact, that were issued, as with other units, these were all questions and issues that were regulated, the kind of conduct and treatment given to terrorists and the civilian population, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Now, on page 2 you say that you took up positions along the blockade line at 6.30 a.m. with a half an hour delay until a connection was made between the platoons in the company and with your left and right neighbours.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes. And I said that my right wing had moved further forward, was almost at the village, so I had to send them back to the blockade line, and that's why there was this delay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And we have a repetition here of what you've already told us. And it says, "During the day, the unit did not engage in any fighting with the Siptar terrorist forces and no civilians were encountered."

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And then the event that took place: The commander of the platoon on the right wing informed you of the shelter and the group that had fled towards Racaj village.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You saw them at the first houses of the village, disappearing between those first houses. And then what do you say in that last paragraph? You say, "Throughout the day, NATO aircraft were flying over the sector where the unit was located, and airstrikes were heard from various directions."

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, the NATO aircraft did fly over the area and struck the Kosare area and that area, too, but from the place that I was at I was not able to see how and where.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: All right. Now, what does that last statement relate to of the 24th of April, the very brief statement on the second day of the operation?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: This statement relates to the fact that the blockade was continued. The units spent the night there at their positions and the blockade continued the next day and ended towards the afternoon, after lunchtime, because the soldiers had their lunch there, and they had dry rations. They had their lunch there, and I remember it at around 1600 hours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is the witness looking at another statement, or --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: It should be tab 8 of Exhibit 321.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Colonel, what are you looking at?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Operations of the unit on the 28th of April.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What's the tab number?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This should be 4A, and it was admitted. It was introduced through General Djosan's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: This should be an order, then, which is admitted, correct. If it is an order.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Is it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: 4A. 4A. It's coming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: Tab 30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, you should be organising your material better than this.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Mr. Kay, tab 30 has a couple of documents of -- couple of statements of Mr. Odak? I think there's only one.

utterances.speaker: MR. KAY
utterances.text: There is only one. I'm just trying to unravel the date. It can be the only one that we're referring to here, tab 30A.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I think I can remember the problem and whether I can solve it, I'm not sure. Originally 30, and thus 30A, contained two statements of this witness, one of the 26th of December relating to the 27th and 28th of April, then I think a shorter statement, which may not have been translated, also of the 26th of December relating to the 28th of April. And I'm holding up what I've got, which is the original -- I mean the B/C/S version. Now, that may still be untranslated, and it may have remained as part of tab 30. My recollection is not absolutely clear on that. There may have been a possibility of it being moved to another tab.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: The Registry's index does not reflect that, so thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have just -- or, rather, that's right. That's the short statement that Mr. Nice had in his hands a moment ago, related to the 28th of April, 1999. And it says, "No English copy" on my copy here, which means it has not been translated. It is a very short statement. Is it on the overhead projector now? Are we seeing it on the ELMO?

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So the date is the 28th of April. It is the second day of the operations. The unit continued its blockade of the territory. There was no -- there were no conflicts with the Siptar terrorist forces today either, nor did they come across civilians at the blockade line. And you go on to tell us what happened -- or, rather, what does this statement say?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: This statement says that the unit continued the activities that it had been engaged in the previous day and that shooting could be heard from the direction of the village of Racaj, Ramoc, and so on, from that general area, and that the action -- or, rather, that I was given the assignment at around 1600 hours, if I remember correctly, because I know the soldiers had already had their lunch, that I should collect up my men and return to the deployment area, the battalion's deployment area. And on that day there was no clash with the terrorists nor did the civilians cross the blockade line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Lieutenant Colonel, in point 105 of the indictment it says, in addition to the forcible expulsion of Kosovo Albanians from the 24th of March, 1999, I assume further on, the forces of the FRY and Serbia also engaged in a number of killings of Kosovo Albanians. Such killings occurred at numerous locations, including ... and I'm going to skip the places that you weren't in and just mention Djakovica, Djakovica being among those places. So please consider that this description, when it comes to you, only refers to Djakovica. So from the 24th of March onwards, our forces, it alleges, and you were in command of them in Djakovica, took part in numerous killings of Kosovo Albanians, a number of killings.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That is absolutely incorrect. There were no killings in the town of Djakovica. I would certainly have known about it, because I was in Djakovica at that time, if there had been.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Now, Witness Beqe Beqaj here said that in August 1998 the population of Racaj left the villages the first time when the army and police reached the area of that particular village and other villages in the valley. Were you there then?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, and I mentioned that when you asked me about 1998.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: I'm asking you about the witness statement now. You were there personally, were you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, the terrorists from the Smonica village withdrew to Racaj. And several days later, when I searched the terrain with the aim of expelling the terrorists from that area, we were in the Racaj village area but there was not a single inhabitant left in the village of Racaj, and I said how the terrorists got rid of the population. The village was completely empty. I didn't come across any terrorists either. The terrorists had withdrawn in the direction of the forest. They'd taken to the forests and wooded areas around Qerim village, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: It's time for the break. We'll adjourn for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, please continue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Mr. Odak, Witness Hani Hoxha stated that on the 27th of March, 1999 -- actually, before I put my question to you, where were you on that date? That's the third day of the war, or the fourth day into the war.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In Djakovica, Mr. Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: On the 27th, around midnight, she heard gunfire, and she saw her neighbour's house on fire, and she went to Milos Gilic 157, where 24 people were hiding, and saw Husein Gashi's body as well as other dead bodies. What happened there? Do you know anything about it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I have no knowledge of any such thing having happened. However, I don't believe it is possible that in the same house in the same building at the same address people be killed twice, because this is also mentioned as having happened on the 1st. I don't have any knowledge of any such thing having happened, and I do not believe that any such thing happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When I first put my question to you it pertains to a paragraph from the indictment, whereas this is the testimony of -- of witness Hani Hoxha. However, this is what matters: You don't have any knowledge of that having happened there? Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 53 of the indictment it says that I, together with others, from the 1st of January, 1999, until the 20th of June, 1999, planned, instigated, ordered, committed, or otherwise aided and abetted in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of terror directed at Kosovo Albanians living in Kosovo in the FRY and that this kind of campaign was carried out with the assistance of the forces of FRY and Serbia that acted against the civilian population in order to expel a large number of Albanians from Kosovo and Metohija in order to establish their own control. Please, you were battalion commander, you were the most senior officer in Djakovica in terms of officers commanding units. Do you know any such thing? Have you ever heard of any such intention, plan, objective, anything from the army of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Everything my unit did, as well as the brigade command, was regulated by orders from the Pristina Corps, that is to say the superior command, and the brigade command then regulated everything through orders. As for battalions and other subordinate units, not in a single document is there any reference to any kind of campaign, violence, murder. That is absolutely incorrect. I know and I'm sure that no such thing happened, nor have I seen a single document regulating something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 55, it says that the forces of FRY and Serbia, in a deliberate and widespread or systematic manner, forcibly expelled and internally displaced hundreds of thousands of Kosovo Albanians from their homes across the entire province of Kosovo, creating an atmosphere of fear and oppression through the use of force, threats of force, and acts of violence. What about you, your unit, and generally speaking in the army? Did you hear anything about force, threats of force, violence, and expelling Albanians from Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: As I've already said, I lived in Kosovo for 13 and a half years. I lived with these people as I did with all other citizens. I'm referring to the Albanians now. And I had very proper relations. And would it be reasonable to expect that I and other people who lived in Djakovica would expel our fellow citizens from the country? I claim that the Albanian population was fleeing exclusively on account of their fear from NATO bombing and threats issued by terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In paragraph 56, it says that throughout Kosovo forces of the FRY and Serbia engaged in a deliberate and widespread or systematic campaign of destruction of property owned by Kosovo Albanian civilians and that this was accomplished by the widespread shelling of towns and villages, the burning and destruction of property, including homes, farms, businesses, cultural monuments and religious sites, and so on and so forth. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: First and foremost, "shelling" is a term I'm unaware of as far as military terminology is concerned. Secondly, all towns were under our control, so it would have been silly for us to shell ourselves, as it is stated here. What happened was that wherever the army of Yugoslavia was, and it was throughout the region of Kosovo and Metohija, NATO aircraft were targeting all these objectives, and they destroyed many villages, and they hit many civilian targets too. So this assertion that we were engaged in shelling, I repeat yet again: We were firing only at buildings from which terrorists were shooting, and they did not hesitate even to use religious buildings, places of worship, for firing from them. For example, the Catholic church in Nec, where I was, they were firing from there too. So we only fired at buildings from which the terrorists fired.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Paragraph 60 says that the forces of FRY and Serbia tried to dissuade Kosovo Albanians from returning to their homes by looting and pillaging the personal and commercial property belonging to them and through wholesale searches, threats of force and acts of violence, et cetera, they expelled them, stole their personal property, including vehicles. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. I don't know about any such thing. After all, it is possible that there were individual cases that were punished. I cannot claim that no such thing ever happened. Certainly there were some isolated individual cases, but whenever a case of that kind was observed, then the law enforcement officials acted against the perpetrators.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Do you know about the seizure of documents from Albanians?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: It was terrorists who were taking these documents away. I personally, in the village of Nec, found over 300 documents. Also in the village of Smonica, a large number of IDs that belonged to Albanians. That is when I talked about the way the terrorists operated. They would come to a village, they would take the documents from the civilian population. I've already talked about this, so I don't need to repeat myself. And they were the only ones who took documents away.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Lieutenant Colonel, what you haven't told us is the source of your information that it was the terrorists who took away the documents. I mean, did you witness this or was this something that you were told?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, I've already mentioned that I personally conducted the action against terrorists in the villages of Nec and Smonica. And I personally, in the house where the commander of this terrorist unit was, found a large number of documents belonging to citizens from Nec. The same goes for Smonica. I collected all these documents and I handed them over to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: When you saying "documents," are you referring to personal identification documents?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes; personal IDs, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, as an officer of the army, did you ever get any order to deport anyone from Kosovo in order to ensure, as it says here, "lasting Serbian control over Kosovo"? Or irrespective of intentions involved, did you ever receive any such orders?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, I've already said a few minutes ago that there was no order of the superior command regulating any such thing, nor did I issue such an order, nor did such things happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any information to the effect that someone had done anything of that sort?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: As an officer and as a battalion commander at the time, did you know what was specifically happening on the ground in the area of Djakovica? Did you know what was happening in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Absolutely. Since there were briefings every day and we reported to the brigade commander, he informed us about the situation on the ground and we reported to him about our own observations from the ground. So we were informed about the situation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: So regarding everything that happened on the ground, you reported to the superior command, the higher instance?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: And did your superiors have information about what was going on through Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, yes. I had meetings with my subordinates every day where I informed them about what happened in our area of responsibility, that is to say the municipality of Djakovica. And they informed me about their observations in the areas where they were, where the -- their company or platoon was deployed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: In these reports did you ever have occasion to see that there was a problem in relation to the civilian population?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: There were absolutely no problems whatsoever. We were neighbours with them, so to speak, and there were no problems of incidents. As far as I know, in the brigades there were two cases where rape was attempted, but these persons were brought into custody by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: You mentioned a while ago, and you said that you lived there for 13 and a half years, that even at the end of the war the town of Djakovica was full of people. Does that mean that the population of Djakovica did not move out?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. Residents of villages came to Djakovica, those who were expelled by terrorists. As I said, probably to portray this image of alleged humanitarian catastrophe.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: According to what you've been saying, Djakovica was full at the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, full, absolutely. When we withdrew, we could barely got out because there were so many people. Had we not been provided security by the Italian soldiers, we could barely withdraw. The town was bursting at the seams.

utterances.speaker: MR. MILOSEVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. I have no further questions. Now other questions will be put to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do I understand you to say that you saw no terrorists being killed throughout this conflict?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: What conflict are you referring to, Mr. Nice?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With NATO, however you described it. Do I understand you to say that you saw no terrorists being killed throughout that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. I did not see a single terrorist killed. It's quite understandable in any army, after all. Terrorists do that too, unfortunately.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... you saw no civilian being killed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You have no explanation that you can offer this Court for any civilians in Djakovica being killed in the course of these events?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: The only civilians I saw killed was the column of civilians moving from Djakovica to Prizren in the month of April that was hit by the NATO Air Force.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We've heard a lot about that. I'm not going to trouble you with that. I'll repeat the question. As to other civilians killed in streets here or there in Djakovica, you have no explanation of any kind that you can give to this Court about how such civilians were killed?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, there was no killing of civilians, nor did I see any civilians that were killed in town. Perhaps these are your assumptions, but it is a fact that this did not happen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll come to that in a short while. I'm a bit confused about your particular position. At some stage you were in charge of part of the anti-aircraft or an anti-aircraft unit, and at some time you were not engaged in anti-aircraft work. Can you just explain it to me a little bit more simply. When were you dealing with anti-aircraft work?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, that is written in one of my statements. Due to certain personnel movements, in September 1998 I was reassigned to be commander of a battalion in the 52nd Artillery Rocket Brigade, and I stayed there until mid-May, the 20th of May, approximately. I can't remember exactly. But I objected to that order. I filed an objection. I did not want to leave my battalion where I had spent 13 years. So I requested to be returned to that other battalion, and I was returned to the battalion at my own request in mid-May, the 2nd Battalion of the 549th Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Throughout your deployment in anti-aircraft and with the brigade, your superior officer was whom?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Colonel Milos Djosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So do you therefore, as a battalion commander, occupy essentially and effectively the same rank, the same level as a witness we've recently heard, Vukovic? You're the same rank as him, are you, battalion commander?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, except that these are battalions for different purposes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes. Therefore we understand from Vukovic that battalions -- or battalion commanders maintain war diaries. Can we see yours?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I don't have this war diary because, I repeat once again, I left that battalion, brigade --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is your war diary, please?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Probably in the archives, because I did not hand over documentation. I left that unit. I left --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There's no reason, is there --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I already said mid-May. And my successor was Major Ramiz Pejcinovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And there is absolutely no reason to believe that that diary no longer exists. It does exist, and you told us you've made no effort to locate it in order to bring it here; is that right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, it's not a question of whether I made an effort or not. First and foremost, I'm an active duty-officer, and I did not have time to gather documentation. You see that I made only three statements. And secondly, I'm sure that this war diary exists but it's in the archives and I really didn't have any time for that. But I could make an effort --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: How many days have you been here preparing to give evidence?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Twenty.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Twenty days. In the course of that time did nobody raise with you, perhaps following questions of earlier witnesses, that it might be desirable for you to lay your hands on contemporaneous documents? Hmm?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I repeat yet again, I was asked -- or, rather, General Djosan, my superior officer, he gathered documents, and at his request, I wrote my statements. So I thought that he would gather all the relevant documentation, because he had the opportunity to do so since he is retired and he has time to do so, whereas as I've already said, I'm a serving officer and --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: As a colonel, you have to simply tell your adjutant, "Lay hold of my diary, will you, please. I want it next week." It's not a very difficult thing to do in a military organisation. Are you really trying to persuade us that it was beyond your ability, for want of time, to get the critical document that would assist this Court?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, Mr. Nice. I'm not trying to persuade you of that at all. I'm repeating this one more time: My superior commander, Colonel, or now General Djosan, asked me to write statements. As for the other documents, I repeat again, since he's a pensioner now and he has time, he was the one who was supposed to gather all these documents, and he did. But he probably did not consider it necessary to look for that diary. I don't know what the reason is.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: At any rate, I did not --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The map that's been --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Just to be clear, we're talking about a diary relating to the 549th Brigade, are we, or --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, his battalion during the conflict when he was a battalion commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, but we're talking -- am I misunderstanding the situation when I think that he was a battalion commander in two battalions?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: He may have been but I'm more particularly concerned -- and to make sure I make this clear to the witness:

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Odak, I'm interested in the time when you were battalion commander between September 1998 and May 1999 in Djakovica. I hope I suggested clearly to you that there was a war diary prepared for that period of time. Am I correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Your Honour, it's that war diary that I'm interested in.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, I follow that, but was General Djosan not with the 549th Brigade, the other -- and therefore in charge of the other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. battalion. So we've been getting answers about a war diary from one brigade to questions from you about the war diary from another brigade, I think. Or another battalion, rather.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me. If I may clarify, with your leave.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1998, I was in a different battalion of the 549th Brigade until September. In that battalion, my superior was then Lieutenant Colonel Vlatko Vukovic. Then in September 1998, I moved to the 52nd Rocket Brigade, and my superior was General Djosan. Then in mid-1999, I moved back to the previous battalion, where my superior was again Vlatko Vukovic. I don't know if I managed to clear things up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: That clarifies it. Obviously the questions and answers were related to the same diary. Thank you, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: We'll try and lay hold of that diary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Can I just ask you, Lieutenant Colonel, in writing your statements, did you rely on your war diary?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You appreciate, don't you, Mr. Odak, that contemporaneous documents are immensely valuable and more valuable than memories that are recorded years later? Do you appreciate and accept that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I accept that. But I remember all those things that matter, the major things.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Help the Court, if you will, please. You've made a number of assertions today, and in respect of each assertion I want you to tell us if you have with you any contemporaneous document recording the assertion you've made. The destruction of the bazaar or marketplace by a bomb, do you have any -- by a NATO bomb. Do you have any contemporaneous document relating to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The destruction of the mosque by a NATO bomb; do you have any contemporaneous document relating to that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't, Mr. Nice, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I'm so sorry, go on.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: But it is certain that in the war diaries of most units you will not find entries about civilian targets because that's not something that you normally enter into war diaries. Those are not normally the type of issues you cover in war diaries. What is recorded are losses and activities conducted by the unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There are other contemporaneous records; combat reports and maybe other documents. Were there combat -- daily combat reports in your battalion?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So they may have recorded what happened at particular locations. I press on. Have you any -- you've made an assertion about Kosovo Albanians somehow taking from other Albanians their documents and destroying them. Is there any contemporaneous document to which you can refer this Court that details that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I didn't say that they destroyed them. The terrorists seized the identification documents of civilians in villages, especially males, able-bodied men capable of fighting, in order to force them to leave the village and join the terrorists. So they didn't destroy their IDs. I said that in Smonica and Nec villages I found a large number of IDs and turned them over to my superior command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: There is a great deal of evidence before this Court from people saying that they had IDs taken from them, either in convoys on the way to borders or at borders, particularly the border with Albania. Can you explain that, or do you say all that evidence must be untrue?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I personally haven't heard of such cases. It's possible that there were individual incidents, but I don't think it was a general occurrence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the fact that you were -- oh, no. You were -- have I got this right: You and your anti-aircraft unit were the only military force in the town of Djakovica at the material time? Have I understood that correctly?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Djakovica housed the command of the 52nd Artillery Rocket Battalion, command battalion, or, rather, their communication company and my battalion, if you're asking about the town of Djakovica itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And the artillery rocket battalion, that's anti-aircraft, is it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And you were anti-aircraft as well, because you were part of an anti-aircraft battalion. Or you were an anti-aircraft battalion, part of a brigade; correct?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. That's not true. Mine was the logistics battalion. The logistics battalion's purpose is to supply ammunition, fuel, food, medical supplies, and other necessities to the units. Therefore, it's not a combat unit but a logistical unit. It has nothing to do with anti-aircraft defence.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Dealing with the period of 1998, and it's the only question I want to ask about 1998, for want of time, Colonel Crosland, an attache at the British embassy, told us that anti-aircraft units had, amongst other things, 20-, 30-, and 40-million cannon. Is he right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, he's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: And of course that cannon's intended for use on aircraft. Is he right about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: In part, because the purpose of those cannons is to fire on targets on the ground and in the air alike.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That was the point he made, and so he seems perhaps to have got it right, has he, because he says he saw anti-aircraft cannon being used quite disproportionately on houses in Kosovo by anti-aircraft units. Is he right on that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, he's not right. I don't know what he means by "disproportionately." They were used to the extent necessary to destroy the terrorists.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, how do you destroy terrorists on the ground with enormous cannon of the type appropriate for aircraft? How do you do it? Focus it on a house and blow the house up?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, we don't shoot at a house. We shoot at a building from which terrorists are firing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Checking first of all that there's nobody but a terrorist in the house before you fire at it with something that's appropriate to knocking a plane out of the sky. Is that what you did?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Nice, I don't know if anybody can possibly know what exactly is located in a building together or behind an enemy. I don't know if NATO was aware what was in the building when they killed the little girl called Milica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, if you'd like to deal with a child, please help me with the following -- I was going to come to this later but I'll deal with it straight away, if I can. We've had a witness in this court, K13, whose statement was permitted to be read to this Court, who was 11 years old at the time of the matters of which she spoke, and she was staying with others in a pool hall, I think for safety. Police came and ordered the occupants out, we were told by this child who was 11 years old at the time. Nobody was questioned. They were simply taken to another house, and in that other house the people, including this girl's family, were shot and killed. Do you know anything about that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, I know nothing about this event. I don't know where it happened, if it happened.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, one possibility I want you to consider before you leave this court is whether in defending the army's position, you're needlessly also defending the police's position. Think about it. Is it possible that the things that are said to have happened in Djakovica were caused by the police and not by the army?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I didn't come here to defend or attack anybody. I am talking about things that I heard and I saw. I gave a solemn declaration and I'm acting accordingly. Those who need to be held liable for committing a crime should be, and should be punished, but I'm certainly not trying to defend anyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... police may have done things unknown to you, and I have your answer. Before I move on, just one other question about documents: You showed us a map -- I'll get the reference for it in a minute. Who made the map?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That map was drawn on the basis of the elements that I provided by General Djosan, as far as I know. I think he drew his own part and Colonel Vukovic drew his part.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Oh, I see. So Djosan and Vukovic were together, and you. Yes?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, they were not working together with me. I'm going to say again: General Djosan just asked me to provide the underlying data, which I did in the form of a statement, and Mr. Djosan was the one who did the drawing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... how did you provide it; in written form or by speaking to him or by doing your own map? Tell us.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: After having been contacted by the expert team, himself, General Djosan, asked me to write these statements and I did. Everything is indicated in those statements, so he could have made the map based on my statements, based on the information in them, because exact trig points are indicated. Those trig points are the dominant features. That's why I remember them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with your information. The expert committee, by the way, just tell us, what did you understand their role to be in all this? Why do you need an expert committee to provide information to a court like this? What did the expert committee do?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I have no information whatsoever about the expert team. All I was told by General Djosan was that it was a team that had been established in order to - how shall I put it? - gain knowledge about certain things, but that's all I know. And I've never been in contact with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: So you provided your statements, and I want to know who drew the plan, the map. Perhaps you don't know.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I've just said I believe it was General Djosan.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Did he do it on his own or did he have a map-maker or did he do it with a colleague? Can you tell us?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I may come back to that. Let's look at a video, please. It's Exhibit 11, shown in the opening of the case but I think the exhibit may have been moved into evidence without either any or much of it being seen. We'll just look at some extracts from it, please. It's a very long video, about an hour, I think in all. I want you to confirm, please, what we're looking at is Djakovica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The video was taken in August of 1999. Is that Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Is that Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I'm not sure about this one.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: What do you say about this damage? Bomb damage or artillery damage or both?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, judging by this damage, I would say artillery weapons do not inflict this kind of damage. These are larger bombs. Probably NATO air bombs because the damage to the buildings is huge.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Tell us, Mr. Odak - You were there, you've told us you're basically the only army officer there - tell us: Bomb or artillery?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I've just told you I was in Djakovica. So it would not have been normal for my army to shell me, as you keep insisting. This can only be a result of NATO air bombs.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Press on, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Robinson, it says here the question: "Press on, please." I haven't heard this question interpreted to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Press on" was a request to Ms. Dicklich to move on with the video.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Very well. Not addressed to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Are you saying that there was no example on any occasion of there being burning of buildings in Djakovica?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, I'm not saying that there were not individual cases - I say that again - but that somebody burnt houses, killed people in the way that you put it, that is incorrect. And I'm sure that all the cases that were uncovered, of course you cannot uncover all cases of crime, so that those which were uncovered were prosecuted, I'm quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Just have a look, please, if you will --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Mr. Nice.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Have a look, please, at a Defence exhibit produced through Stevanovic, D299, tab 72, and if you just look at paragraph 12 of this record of the Ministry of Interior's meeting held on the 11th of May of 1999. The MUP, the police -- and I'll get the usher to put it on the overhead projector at page 12 of the English. It's not on my screen, I'm afraid. Have you got the end of paragraph 12 where we're looking at the report of Brigade Commander Colic?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Does the Court have it on its screen? I don't have it on mine, I'm afraid. Well, to save time I'll read out to you what's in English -- there it is. Thank you very much, perfectly positioned, don't move it. Bottom of the screen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "Commander Colic reported this: Citizens and refugees in Djakovica town were treated correctly during the operations, however, after all the actions, VJ reservists burnt houses and went into them; we informed VJ commanders in order to prevent these incidents." Were, at a minimum, VJ reservists burning houses, as the police seem to have recorded against you? Yes or no.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, cooperation between the army and the police was on a daily basis. Now, this vision of the brigade commander or, rather, this meeting with the brigade commander and the responsible people of the MUP in Djakovica were on a daily basis. They had regular meetings and just as they helped us uncover individual crimes, we would help them uncover individual crimes. Specifically speaking, I'm quoting the example of these two once again, the two soldiers that tried -- that attempted rape from our brigade. Those two cases. But we received information about that from the MUP organs. Now, as to this particular instance, well, it is possible -- I say they were individual cases, but he informed us of this for us to be able to take steps in the best intentions.
