But that certainly didn't happen in my unit and with the knowledge of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Where is the record of the prosecutions?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, the command of the brigade sent them on. That's up to the brigade command.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... this Court of the prosecutions of people for burning houses down in Djakovica, if there is a record. It doesn't exist, does it, Mr. Odak?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, no, we didn't have such cases, Mr. Nice, that there were any burnings of houses. I mentioned the only two cases that I know happened in the brigade, and steps were taken against those individuals. Criminal reports were filed and they were taken into custody. But there was no burning of houses in the unit at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You've told us about the rapes before and we don't know what happened to the alleged rapist. Or perhaps we do; nothing. But there was Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. one other trial, I mentioned it to the previous witness, Mancic. Do you remember the trial of Mancic? Do you remember the trial of Mancic, the officer?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, I didn't follow that.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Well, did you hear about it at all? Did you understand that his trial came about only because one of them --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Sorry?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You did hear about it. And the only reason he was put on trial is because one of the men he told to kill Albanians reported himself for process and therefore there had to be a trial. Do you remember that happening?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I do remember, but --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: -- that trial -- well, I have my opinions about that trial. I don't want to present them here and now, because it was an officer of mine, and as far as I know, the lawyers received from KFOR the fact that these people did not exist at all. So that particular trial was mounted, in my opinion.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Let me just go back to the point which I think you confirmed: The Mancic trial is a trial where there had to be a trial because one of the people he'd commanded to commit a crime reported himself. He couldn't avoid having a trial. And it's only in special circumstances that there was any judicial process for the crimes that were being committed in Kosovo during this period. Am I not right?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Well, let me tell you. You -- I didn't follow that trial very much because the goal was clear to me. And all I can talk about is what happened in my own unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Before we move to the next topic, just a little bit more from the video. But before we look at a couple of things from the video, tell me this: Are you saying there was no expressed hostility towards Albanians, no expressed desires to get them out or to do damage to them in this period between March and May of 1999 or March and June?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In -- you accept there was hostility, do you?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, no. I said there was no hostility. Or perhaps there were individual cases, but that the general mood was that way, that's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Can you read this out for us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: "Lepa sela lepo gore"; "Beautiful village, beautiful woods."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... villages burn nicely. Ugly ones stay ugly when they're burning. Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: "Pretty villages burnt nicely," is what it says, and that was a film that had that same title, "Lepa sela lepo gore," and that was uttered by one of the actors in the film.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: I see. Let's look at the next one, then.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: "Nice villages burn nicely."

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: The next one. Does this express the desire, "Serbia until Tirane, fuck you, NATO." Is that what it says?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: "What's going to happen to this house? I'll set fire to it." Is that what that one says?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... was a town full of hate, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, that's not true that it was full of hate. Let me repeat again. I was there for 13 and a half years. I lived with the people and it was impossible for me to live amongst people like that and to hate them. And these graffiti mean nothing. The war is a special state where people express some of their feelings which are not or certainly are not normal in any way during those times. So this means absolutely nothing.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: You appreciate, don't you, that as well as witnesses who have come to this Court, events in Djakovica have been logged by several other organisations, including Human Rights Watch and OSCE. Do you appreciate that?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Now, help me with this as a person who knows your Djakovica, or knew it: Was there a man called Dr. Izet Hima, a very respected physician? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Do you remember --

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't know him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know a man Qamil Zherka, who was aged 70, and his son Nexhdet, aged 41?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, Djakovica has a population of 60.000, and the municipality has over a hundred thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: So --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... if you know these people. Do you know a then-prominent lawyer called Urim Rexha? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Finally, do you remember a man called Mark Malota, who rented his house to the Mother Teresa Society? Do you remember him?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No, no. No, I don't know the individual.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... two passages then of a book called "Under Orders." We don't have time to go into more, but if we can just show you, please, on the overhead projector, it's in English and I'll read the passage slowly to you. One organisation, Human Rights Watch, and this is Exhibit number -- I always forget the number. Don't worry. I'll come back to the exhibit number. This book, which is based on extensive interviews which are footnoted, has a large passage on Djakovica. It's Exhibit 145. And it summarises the position in this way: "Djakovica suffered the most intense violence against civilians of Kosovo's larger cities. While not all of the city's estimated 100.000 residents (including 20.000 internally displaced) were expelled, threats and killing drove a majority of the population from the city. Serbian police and paramilitaries, as well as Yugoslav soldiers, killed approximately 200 people between March 24 and June 12 alone in the city, and many more were killed in nearby villages such as Meja and Korenica. Approximately 1.200 other people from the Djakovica municipality remained missing as of February 2000. At least 150 ... were arrested during the war and taken to Serbia proper where they were convicted by Serbian courts for terrorist acts, although most were later released." Now, that's a summary, of course. Do you say there's truth in that or not a word of truth?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, if the source of this is a veteran of the KLA, Mr. Oker [phoen], then it's certainly not true. None of this is true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Mr. Who?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: I don't know about any of this. Mr. Walker. Mr. Walker. If his organisation is the source of this, then it certainly isn't true. Because I don't know any of this, about any of this.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: First of all, this organisation has nothing to do with Mr. Walker. But since you mention Mr. Walker, is it going to be your position if and when we look at any document that has any connection with Mr. Walker, that anything remotely connected by Mr. Walker is false from first to last? Is that going to be your case, your position?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, the person whom terrorists call their own veteran, I have reason to doubt any of his documents or any of his words.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: Very well. This book, which has nothing to do with Mr. Walker, it comes from Human Rights Watch, which published reports sent to the accused on a regular basis throughout the 1990s, deals with Djakovica in some detail but let's go, if the usher would be good enough, to page 216.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, this is a day when we'll have to stop at 1.43.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: They -- they analyse available evidence about Djakovica in various phases, and this is why I asked you about the names I asked you about. It says that "The first wave of violence began on March the 24th when NATO initiated its attack on Yugoslavia, and it continued until the 2nd of April." It deals with the mosque, which it says was set on fire, and it deals with sporadic killings. It then says this: "On March 25, unknown security forces broke into the home of a respected physician ... and shot him in front of his wife." That's Dr. Hima. "According to the Washington Post, Faton Poloshka picked up Dr. Hima's body at 5.00 p.m. and then collected the bodies of three other ethnic Albanians killed that day: Kujtim Dula ... Qamil Zherka -" the man aged 70 - "and his son, Nexhdet." Then this: "Prominent Djakovica residents Urim Rexha, a lawyer, and Mark Malota, an LDK leader who rented his house to the Mother Teresa Society, were also killed." Then it goes on to March the 26th. You were there on this day. Under cover of NATO's attack, the opportunity was taken to pick off prominent Kosovo Albanian residents and kill them, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: That's your insinuation. It's not true.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: That's why I asked you. Were you completely unaware of this group of either respected or certainly well known and significant local residents, were you unaware that they were all killed on that day?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, at the time, I was battalion commander, and I had many things to attend to and one of those things was to protect 40 tonnes of explosives which could have blown up the whole of Djakovica. So I didn't delve in questions like that nor did I hear anything like that happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: In my remaining one minute, let's go back to two things you said and see if you want to review them. In answer to the accused, you've told us that you knew everything that happened in Djakovica, and nothing happened. In answer to me, you declined to take the opportunity to blame police or other forces. Now, is the reality you haven't the first idea what was happening in the centre of Djakovica or in its residential areas on the 24th of March 1999 because you were elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: No. I was in Djakovica. I said that, and I have no reason to protect anyone, let me state that again. I do not say there were not individual cases, but there was -- that there was organised operations such as some unknown police unit, there were no such units. All police units that were there were properly trained and clothed, and their most important task was to provide security for the civilian population and to prevent crime in town.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: With Ms. Dicklich's assistance and the Court's indulgence, one more question. Please turn over one page and put the -- one page, please. This is a picture of the 20 people killed, their bodies burned in the house at 163 Milos Gilic Street, and we can see from the picture how many of them are young children. You were there. You were the senior military person. Explain that to us, please.

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: These are really terrible pictures, and certainly the crimes like that and similar crimes must be punished just like the crime --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ...

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: -- of the column of civilians that was hit. However --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICE
utterances.text: No, Mr. Odak, you will not escape by referring to NATO. You were there, you've told this accused you basically know everything that happened and that nothing happened. You tell us, please, how were those children killed and what's been done, if anything, to bring the culprits to justice?

utterances.speaker: ZLATKO ODAK
utterances.text: Mr. Nice, I said that my subordinates passed by during that period of time that is mentioned in the indictment, they passed through the area and noticed nothing. Therefore, I cannot tell you anything else except for the report or, rather, what my subordinate officer informed me of. And I don't believe that he lied, that he would have lied to me had he seen something along the way, en route. I see no reason for him to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We have to take the adjournment now, but Judge Bonomy has a question for the accused.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Milosevic, just clarification on one thing from earlier this morning. You presented us with a number of medical reports from experts. One of these is by a Professor Vukasin Andric. Now, earlier this year we heard evidence from a Professor Vukasin Andric. Is it the same person?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, the same person, and he is a very distinguished otorhinolaryngologist. And it has nothing to do -- the examination, ear, nose, and mouth, has nothing to do with the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: We're adjourned until tomorrow, 9.00 a.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ROBINSON
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Wednesday, the 16th day of November, 2005, at 9.00 a.m.

procedural_notes.text: --- Whereupon the hearing adjourned at 1.46 p.m.,
